opus-5.5.text:
Well, the idea of the T is that you want both breadth and depth. The vertical bar of the T is depth: you should be really, truly expert in at least one area. In my case, early on, that was computer vision, and within that, specific problems like edge detection, texture, and segmentation. You need to know that area well enough that you can push the frontier. You know the literature, you know the techniques, and you have the taste to tell which problems are worth working on.

But the horizontal bar matters just as much, and I think young researchers sometimes neglect it. That's breadth: knowing enough about neighboring fields to draw on them. For AI, that might mean some neuroscience, some cognitive science and psychology, some optimization and statistics, some control theory, and some knowledge of what's happening in natural language or robotics if you're a vision person. Many of the most interesting ideas come from importing a concept from one field into another. A lot of my own work was inspired by thinking about human vision and perception, by reading people like Gibson or the Gestalt psychologists, or by looking at what neurophysiologists were finding.

The field also changes. If you are only deep and narrow, then when a paradigm shift comes, and we've seen several in AI with the deep learning revolution and now large models, you can find yourself stranded. If you have breadth, you can recognize where things are going and reposition yourself. You can carry your deep expertise into the new paradigm instead of being made obsolete by it.

So my advice to someone starting out is this. Pick something and go really deep, because that's how you make real contributions and earn credibility. But keep reading broadly, keep talking to people outside your immediate subfield, and stay curious. In the long run, that combination is what lets you do work that is both rigorous and original.

r001.rationale: The candidate says breadth helps researchers adapt to paradigm shifts and carry their expertise into new paradigms, and that breadth combined with depth enables rigorous, original work over the long run.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the T model is this idea that you should have breadth, that's the horizontal bar of the T, and then depth in one area, which is the vertical stem. And I think for someone starting out in AI research, both of those matter, but for different reasons.

The depth is what makes you a researcher at all. You have to go deep enough in something, whether it's vision, or learning theory, or robotics, that you actually understand the problem from the inside. You know what's been tried, you know why things fail, you have taste about what's a real contribution and what's just noise. That kind of taste only comes from really living inside a problem for a while. You can't get it from reading survey papers.

But the breadth is what keeps you from becoming obsolete, and frankly it's where a lot of the good ideas come from. Our field moves very fast. When I started out, computer vision and machine learning were almost separate communities. Now they're completely intertwined, and robotics is coming in, and language models are coming in. If you only knew one thing deeply and nothing else, you'd have a hard time recognizing when a tool from a neighboring area is exactly what your problem needs. Many of the biggest advances in vision came from people importing ideas, from statistics, from neuroscience, from signal processing.

The other thing I'd say is that breadth gives you a sense of what questions are worth asking. If you know a bit of psychology and neuroscience, you have a different view of what perception is for than if you've only ever thought about benchmarks. That shapes the problems you choose, and choosing good problems is probably the most important skill in research.

So my advice to students is, pick your stem early enough that you can get really good at it, but don't let the stem become a silo. Go to talks outside your area. Read things that don't immediately seem relevant. Over time the breadth starts to pay off in ways you couldn't have predicted.

r001.rationale: The candidate says breadth helps researchers recognize useful ideas from neighboring fields, generate better questions, and stay relevant as AI changes; it adds that breadth pays off over time.

astra-6.text:
I like the T model because you need both breadth and depth. The horizontal bar is a broad understanding of the field, and the vertical bar is deep expertise in something particular. If you have only breadth, you may know the vocabulary of many areas, but you haven’t learned how to push beyond what is already known. Going deep on a problem teaches you what research actually involves: questioning assumptions, dealing with failures, and figuring out whether an idea really works.

But depth alone can leave you isolated. In AI, ideas connect across vision, language, robotics, learning, and other disciplines. Breadth helps you recognize those connections and ask better questions. So, for somebody starting out, I would encourage broad learning while choosing a problem on which to develop real depth. You don’t have to become an expert in everything, but you should be able to learn from people whose expertise is different from yours.

r001.rationale: The response says breadth helps researchers recognize connections and ask better questions, but it does not state that greater breadth enables greater contributions over the long term.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the T model captures a useful balance. The vertical part of the T means that you know one subject deeply enough to do serious research—to get beyond the textbook and understand where the difficult, unanswered questions are. The horizontal part means that you have enough breadth to recognize connections to other areas and to talk to people working on different problems.

For someone starting in AI, both matter. If you only have breadth, you may know the vocabulary of many fields without being able to contribute to any of them. But if you specialize too narrowly, you may miss an idea from another field that would help you solve your problem. So develop depth in something, while remaining curious about mathematics, computer science, neuroscience, and the world your systems are meant to operate in.

r001.rationale: The response says breadth can help researchers recognize connections and find ideas that help solve a problem, but it does not state that greater breadth enables more contribution over the long term.
